extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate mathematics students, early-career mathematicians, and researchers seeking career/research advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and quality standards for succeeding as a research mathematician (study habits, research practice, exposition, professional behavior, career decisions). Targeted at students and early-career researchers in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance intuition and rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine rigorous formal thinking with good intuition; use rigour to destroy bad intuition while clarifying and elevating good intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once comfortable with rigorous thinking, revisit your intuitions and use formal skills to test and refine them. The ideal state is when heuristic arguments naturally suggest rigorous counterparts and vice versa. Avoid discarding intuition entirely or treating intuition as 'non-rigorous' and therefore worthless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition beyond grades/exams to conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from undergraduate habits of memorisation and exam-focused study to self-motivated study, experimentation, and doing mathematics at a deeper level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop intellectual and intuitive thought rather than focusing on artificial benchmarks. Revise undergraduate study habits and cultivate independent reading and experimentation to advance understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard (consistent sustained effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious research requires a large amount of reading and writing; breakthroughs are largely a product of hard work directed by experience and intuition rather than sudden 'Eureka' moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read all relevant literature, write sketches and detailed treatments, and not rely solely on intelligence or last-minute efforts. The devil is in the details: be prepared to fill in substantial detail and supporting evidence for ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and work in areas of mathematics you enjoy, as enjoyment helps sustain the long-term energy required for research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer working in areas you find interesting over working where something is merely fashionable. Enjoyment increases the chance of sustained effort and long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't base career decisions on glamour or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid selecting fields, problems, or departments solely because they are glamorous or famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glamorous areas are highly competitive and require strong backgrounds; famous problems are rarely solved without long preparation on simpler problems. Do not chase prizes or recognition as primary goals; instead, produce good mathematics and recognition will follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing learning is essential—even in your specialty; revisit basic results, understand hypotheses, look for alternative proofs, generalizations, and model examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecture or write expository material (even for yourself) to internalize difficult results. Ask questions like when a lemma is applicable, necessity of hypotheses, analogues in other areas, and connections to broader paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be afraid to learn outside your field
rubrics_metrics.description: If progress requires external mathematics, learn it—expanding your range makes your work more interesting and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When other areas are active, learn why they're interesting and what techniques or phenomena they offer. Cross-field knowledge helps when similar problems or obstructions appear in your own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the limitations of your tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Know when your preferred methods do not work and what their obstructions are, to avoid wasting time and to hunt for new tools or problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a library of counterexamples and model situations. Know when tools can be substituted and the comparative trade-offs. If you treat a tool as a 'magic wand', that's a sign you need deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the power of others' tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Study unfamiliar techniques used by others, locate simple model cases where those tools are effective, and compare strengths/weaknesses to your own methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out the simplest non-trivial example for the new tool; practice until you can add it to your repertoire. This prepares you to recall and apply the tool when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'dumb' questions and explore failed lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Be unafraid to ask naïve or simple questions (delete a hypothesis, attempt a different method) since exploring failed avenues illuminates why conventions exist and deepens understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such questions may occasionally lead to surprising conclusions but usually reveal why conventional wisdom holds; they are essential in learning the relative power of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Critically test your solutions and methods; look for counterexamples or consequences that would indicate flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a method proves too much (e.g., implies false stronger statements), there is likely a flaw. When a solution seems effortless, re-analyse and try to find counterexamples or obstructions as diagnostic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead (purpose-driven lemma/problem design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always ask how an intermediate result (lemma) will be used: which features matter, whether a weaker lemma suffices, and whether the statement can be simplified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to small claims and big theorems. Reformulating a target statement before proving it can save time and produce optimal statements that are easier to prove or apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly go to talks and conferences, even outside your immediate area, to learn techniques, make connections, and discover perspectives relevant to your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern mathematics is collaborative—know who's who and what's happening. You need not understand everything in a talk; learning something is valuable. Bringing your own work to quietly work on while not following a talk is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study at different institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do graduate/postdoctoral study at different places than prior training to broaden education and expose yourself to different mathematical cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moving institutions also helps the psychological transition in career stages and exposes you to strengths not available at a single department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Your advisor understands your situation best—keep them informed about your availability and progress, and seek their guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If advisor is unavailable or relationship is poor, regularly consult at least one other experienced mathematician. Give advance warning for long absences from studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the initiative (self-directed work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on your advisor; proactively research, read, talk to peers, and write when you feel the need to learn or produce something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use library/internet resources, discuss with other students or faculty, and pursue learning or writing projects on your own initiative (see 'ask yourself dumb questions').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be patient with research progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that most problems require months (or longer) of patient work; lack of visible progress is common and often precedes breakthroughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the field or you are not ready for a problem, set it aside and build skills on related problems. Avoid discouragement over absence of quick 'Eureka' moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible in research directions and career plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is unpredictable—be prepared to change directions, update goals, and not base career decisions on a single faculty member or fixed plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publicly committing to a famous problem without a feasible plan. In grant proposals, claim big goals only if you have coherent plans and track records; otherwise give milestones and feasible subproblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional in conduct and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Take duties seriously, maintain neutral and professional tone in writing, be generous and correct in credit and acknowledgements, and manage setbacks constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid frivolity in professional contexts; separate personal content from professional pages; don't be overly self-promoting; treat rejections and errors as learning opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be considerate of your audience in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a good-faith effort to communicate results to the intended audience: logical layout, notation choice, and adding informal/heuristic motivation are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good paper should tell the reader 'Why' and 'Where' as well as 'How' and 'What'. Devote effort to introductions, overviews, and signposting. Sit on a paper and reread with fresh eyes to spot exposition flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't prematurely obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid focusing exclusively on a very difficult problem before you have the preparation and career stability to afford that risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep big problems in mind but spend most time on feasible 'low-hanging fruit' to build experience, credibility, and a track record before committing heavily to speculative grand projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat talks differently from papers
rubrics_metrics.description: A talk should complement a paper with a high-level, informal overview and not be a verbatim presentation of a paper's technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving talks that are merely transparencies of your paper. Make talks friendly to non-experts by covering background and basic examples early. Use techniques like proving a standard theorem X in the style of Y as preparation for proving new theorem Y in the talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the wastebasket (prune and rewrite aggressively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to scale down, refocus, shelve, or completely rewrite projects and drafts when they are not working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know when to persist and when to be pragmatic. Back up work before major rewrites. Keep even wrong pieces archived in case salvageable material appears later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down what you've done (record sketches and tricks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record sketches of arguments and tricks in durable form so you can reconstruct them later and free mental space for new learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even informal writeups help practice TeX and expository writing, test understanding, and serve as sources for later papers, notes, or proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your work available (use preprint servers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post preprints online (e.g., arXiv) so others can find and build upon your work; priority is preserved by timestamps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure preprints are reasonably polished though they can be updated. Email preprints to experts only when unquestionably of direct interest to avoid appearing pushy; typically making work available online suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize competitions are different from research
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical competitions are fun but different from graduate-level research; do not expect the same problem flavour or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition-style problem-solving may help with some steps, but most research requires patient literature reading, applying known techniques, trying model problems, and developing intuition over longer time scales. Enjoy competitions but don't neglect the 'boring' aspects of education that are ultimately more useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify understanding by reading literature and writing detailed sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think you understand something, back it up by reading relevant literature and writing at least a sketch or eventual complete treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice tests your grasp of details and prepares you to turn intuition into publishable, verifiable results; do not rely on superficial understanding.
